Before going into the different uses, understand this single idea that ties them all together:

"Past" always means "beyond a point."

That point can be a location, a moment in time, a number, an age, a stage, or even a limit of human ability. Once something is past a point, it has already crossed that point and left it behind. Everything else in this explanation is just this same idea applied to different situations.

This is the most visual use. When a person or thing moves from one side of a fixed object to the other side — and keeps going — they go past it.

  • She walked past the bakery.

She walked in front of the bakery and continued beyond it. She didn't stop. She didn't go inside. She simply moved forward and the bakery was left behind her.

  • The train rushed past the small village without stopping.
  • A dog ran past me at full speed.
  • He drove past the turning and had to come back.

The key thing here is continuous movement beyond the reference point. The person or object doesn't stay at the location — they go through it and beyond.

"Past" can also describe a static position — where something is, not where it's going. Here it means: on the far side of something, after you have crossed a certain point.

  • The pharmacy is just past the traffic light.

This means: keep going, cross the traffic light, and then you will find the pharmacy on the other side of it.

  • His house is past the bridge.
  • The school is about two kilometres past the roundabout.

You use this sense when giving directions. It tells someone: go beyond this landmark, and then you'll reach what you're looking for.

"Past" is very commonly used to talk about time. The idea is the same — you have gone beyond a certain moment on the clock or in the day.

Telling the time:

In English, we express minutes after the hour using "past."

  • It's ten past seven. → It is 10 minutes beyond 7 o'clock. (7:10)
  • It's half past three. → It is 30 minutes beyond 3 o'clock. (3:30)
  • It's a quarter past nine. → It is 15 minutes beyond 9 o'clock. (9:15)

This is extremely common in British English. The minutes are counted as going past the hour, i.e., beyond it.

Beyond a general time:

  • It was past midnight when she finally arrived. → It was later than midnight.
  • Don't stay out past ten o'clock. → Don't stay out beyond ten o'clock.
  • By the time we reached the hospital, it was well past noon.

"Well past" is used to emphasise that something is far beyond a certain time — not just slightly after it.
4. Beyond a Number, Age, or Stage

"Past" works the same way with numbers and ages — it means you have exceeded or gone beyond them.

Age:

  • She's past sixty. → She is older than sixty. She has crossed that age and gone beyond it.
  • He's past retirement age. → He has exceeded the age at which people retire.
  • The patient is past the age where surgery is advisable.

Stages and conditions:

  • The milk is past its best. → The milk has gone beyond its best point. It is no longer at peak freshness.
  • The house is past its prime. → The house has gone beyond its best years. It is now in decline.
  • He is past his peak as an athlete. → He has gone beyond his best period of performance.
  • The project is past the planning stage. → The planning stage is over; it has been crossed and left behind.
  • The patient is past the critical stage. → The most dangerous stage has been passed through and is now behind them.
5. Beyond Someone's Ability, Endurance, or Understanding

This is a more abstract but very important use. When something exceeds what a person can do, understand, believe, or endure, we say it is past them or past a certain faculty.

  • It's past me why anyone would do that. → I cannot understand why anyone would do that. It exceeds my ability to understand.
  • It's past belief. → It goes beyond what is possible to believe. It is unbelievable.
  • The pain was past bearing. → The pain exceeded what could be endured. It was unbearable.
  • The noise was past all tolerance. → The noise exceeded any reasonable level of tolerance.
  • She was past caring about what others thought.

That last example is subtle and worth noting. "Past caring" means she has reached a point so far beyond caring that she simply no longer cares at all. It implies that there was a time when she did care, but she has moved so far beyond that point that it no longer applies to her.
6. "I Wouldn't Put It Past Someone" — A Fixed Phrase

This is a set phrase that uses "past" to mean beyond what someone is capable of — specifically, beyond what you would expect from them as a moral or ethical limit.

  • I wouldn't put it past him to lie about his qualifications.

This means: I believe he is capable of lying about his qualifications. It would not surprise me. The idea is that the behaviour is not beyond his limits — it is actually within what he might do.

This phrase is always used in the negative: "I wouldn't put it past..." You are saying that their possible bad behaviour is not past them — it is within their range.

Another example:

  • Would she really betray her own team? I wouldn't put it past her.
7. "Past" Telling You Something Is Over or No Longer Applies

Sometimes "past" carries the meaning that something has already gone by and can no longer be acted on.

  • It's past the deadline. → The deadline has already been crossed. The time for it is gone.
  • That's all in the past now. (Here "past" is a noun, but the idea is the same.)
  • Those opportunities are past. (Here it functions as an adjective.)

As a preposition specifically:

  • We are well past the point of no return. → We have gone so far beyond the point of no return that going back is impossible.
  • It's past the point where apologies will help. → Apologies can no longer help; the situation has moved too far beyond that.

This is one of the most common mistakes in English, and you must understand the difference clearly.

  • "Past" is the preposition (and also an adjective, noun, or adverb). It is never a verb.
  • "Passed" is the past tense of the verb "to pass."

Look at these two sentences — they describe the same event but use different words:

  • She walked past the school. → "past" is a preposition. The verb is "walked."
  • She passed the school. → "passed" is the verb. There is no preposition.

The test is simple: if there is already a verb in the sentence (walked, ran, drove, flew), then you need the preposition past. If "pass" is itself the main verb, then you conjugate it to passed.

  • ❌ He drove passed the gate. (wrong — "drove" is the verb, so you need the preposition "past")
  • ✅ He drove past the gate. (correct)
  • ✅ He passed the gate. (correct — "passed" is the verb)

No matter how "past" is used as a preposition, the meaning is always the same underneath: a point has been crossed and left behind.

SituationWhat the "point" is

When you walk past a shop, the shop is the point you crossed. When it is past midnight, midnight is the time you crossed. When someone is past sixty, sixty is the age they crossed. When something is past bearing, the limit of endurance is the point that was crossed. The preposition always signals: we are on the far side of something.

Once you see "past" this way — as a word that places you beyond a specific point — every use of it will feel natural and logical.
